Code-switching. The practice of alternating between two or more languages or dialects within a single conversation or even a single sentence. Multilingual speakers employ code-switching strategically to navigate different social contexts, express identity, or convey meaning that a single code cannot capture. Rather than a deficit or confusion, code-switching is a sophisticated linguistic resource and a window into how language intertwines with identity and community.

Bilingual and multilingual speakers code-switch routinely. It is not a sign of linguistic confusion but rather evidence of linguistic competence, the ability to deploy multiple codes appropriately. Situational code-switching shifts which language is used based on context. Speakers might use the heritage language at home, English at school, and Spanish with friends, selecting the appropriate code for the audience and setting.

Intra-sentential code-switching, switching within a single sentence, requires deep grammatical knowledge of both languages. Linguists initially thought such mixing was impossible, but research proved it follows systematic rules. Code-switching serves social functions. Marking group identity. Creating solidarity with others who share multilingualism. Establishing social distance. It signals us and them linguistically.

Prestige hierarchies shape code-switching. Speakers often shift toward higher-prestige codes, colonial languages and standard varieties, in formal contexts and toward vernacular codes in casual settings, reflecting broader power structures. Heritage language speakers often code-switch to accommodate monolingual listeners or because they are more fluent in one language for certain domains, technical terms in English but family vocabulary in the heritage language.

Colonial and postcolonial contexts intensify code-switching. Formerly colonized peoples navigate languages imposed by colonizers alongside ancestral languages, with code-switching becoming a daily linguistic reality. Language contact itself drives code-switching. When communities speak multiple languages, speakers develop code-switching norms that become part of the group's linguistic identity, as with Spanglish in US Hispanic communities.
